Fig. 3 | The translational vector for tissue-engineered cartilage products.
The translational vector is the process from research and development to clinical use, and it requires the fulfilment of multiple steps in the domains of regulation, manufacturing, and funding and intellectual property (IP). a. The aspects of the translational vector must be coordinated in parallel as they influence each other simultaneously in an interconnected manner. For example, an investigator might only be able to secure the appropriate funding to conduct costly clinical trials after IP is established. b. In the USA, the multiple successive steps of regulatory approval required for development of biologics or devices for cartilage tissue engineering are managed by the Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) or the Center for Devices and Radiological Health (CDRH), respectively. c. Successive stages in the manufacture of tissue-engineered cartilage products (for use in animal studies, clinical trials and clinical-grade products) are each subject to specific manufacturing quality requirements. d. Translation of a product from research to clinical use requires escalating funding and appropriate management of IP. BLA, Biologics License Application; GLP, Good Laboratory Practice; GMP, Good Manufacturing Practice; IDE, Investigational Device Exemption; IND, Investigational New Drug; PMA, Premarket Approval.
